DOCUMENT R03 — Transmission fault and protection records, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: National Grid Electricity Transmission (NGET); lightning detection data: MeteoGroup
Record type: compiled circuit fault, protection, auto-reclose, power quality and lightning records
STATUS: RECONSTRUCTED FOR EVALUATION FROM PUBLISHED RECORDS — NOT AN ORIGINAL SYSTEM EXPORT.
Entries are compiled from published post-event investigation reports; layout and wording are reconstructions.
Sections A-F are records; section G holds later, attributed assessments.
Clock reference: BST (UTC+01:00). The sources do not label the clock of the B3 and section C times; they are
read as BST because the ESO report dates this event at 4:52pm, and are written with +01:00. Times with no
such anchor (B2, section E) are marked "clock basis not stated" and are written without an offset.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated by the record owner in published material;
[estimated] value the record owner describes as an estimate; [measured] and [illustrative] not used.

SECTION A — CIRCUIT AND NETWORK CONTEXT
A1  Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main: 400 kV [reported] double-circuit overhead line of just over 35 km [reported],
    from Eaton Socon substation (near St Neots, Cambridgeshire) to Wymondley Main substation (near Stevenage,
    Hertfordshire). Lattice steel towers carry two circuits, each with 3 [reported] conductors (phases) on one
    side of the tower, and an earth wire at the top of the tower.
A2  Planned outage on 9 August 2019: the Killingholme–Keadby circuit was out of service for planned
    maintenance; the NGET power quality monitor connected to it, close to Killingholme, was unavailable.

SECTION B — LIGHTNING DETECTION RECORDS (MeteoGroup data, as reported by ESO and NGET)
B1  9 August 2019, 24 hours [reported]: 12,370 [reported] lightning strikes across mainland UK.
B2  2 hours [reported] preceding 17:00 [reported] (clock basis not stated): 2,106 [reported] strikes across
    mainland UK.
B3  2019-08-09T16:52:33+01:00 [reported]: three [reported] almost simultaneous lightning strikes recorded
    adjacent to the Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit, close to Willian Arboretum, at the Wymondley end of the
    circuit.
B4  Location uncertainty: each strike is plotted with a radius of uncertainty for the location of the direct
    hit; any of the three strikes could have hit the circuit.
B5  Largest of the three strikes: current amplitude 33.7 kA [reported].
B6  NGET overlay of MeteoGroup activity near the circuit: a number of strikes close to NGET overhead line
    circuits; one strike is timed at the same time as the fault; the activity aligns with protection data
    indicating the fault was 4.5 km [reported] from Wymondley Main, just outside Letchworth Garden City.

SECTION C — FAULT AND PROTECTION RECORD, EATON SOCON–WYMONDLEY MAIN CIRCUIT (times read as BST, +01:00)
C1  2019-08-09T16:52:33.490+01:00 [reported]: fault inception. Single (blue) phase to earth fault on one Eaton
    Socon–Wymondley circuit: the middle conductor (blue phase) faulted to the earthed tower.
C2  Fault location: approximately 4.5 km [reported] along the circuit from the Wymondley Main end.
C3  Fault infeed: approximately 21 kA (RMS) [reported] from Wymondley Main; approximately
    7 kA (RMS) [reported] from Eaton Socon.
C4  Blue-phase voltage during the fault: estimated 50% [estimated] depression (ESO timeline); NGET: circa
    50% [reported] at the fault location, lasting 100 ms [reported] in the vicinity of the fault.
C5  2019-08-09T16:52:33.560+01:00 [reported]: Wymondley Main end opens to clear the fault; main protection
    operating time 70 ms [reported] after fault inception.
C6  2019-08-09T16:52:33.564+01:00 [reported]: Eaton Socon end opens to clear the fault; main protection
    operating time 74 ms [reported] after fault inception.
C7  Requirement cited by NGET, Grid Code Connection Condition CC.6.2.3.1.1, primary protection fault clearance
    times: 80 ms at 400 kV [reported]; 100 ms at 275 kV [reported]; 120 ms at 132 kV and below [reported].
C8  2019-08-09T16:52:53+01:00 [reported]: Eaton Socon–Wymondley circuit energised on Delayed Auto-Reclose
    (DAR), returning it to service about 20 seconds [reported] after the fault.
C9  DAR was available and in service on the circuit. After the reclose the network was in the same
    configuration as before the event; no further operational intervention or immediate site attendance was
    required.

SECTION D — POWER QUALITY AND VOLTAGE RECORDS (measured magnitudes as published; assessments are in G)
D1  Ryhall 400 kV [reported] (the next substation along from Eaton Socon): blue-phase voltage depression
    44% [reported]; duration of the event including voltage recovery 100 ms [reported].
D2  Ryhall: a further small transient after the fault; NGET text: a minute [reported] after the fault;
    figure annotation: 2 mins [reported] after the fault. It did not register at Necton.
D3  Necton 400 kV [reported] (Norfolk; electrically further from the fault): blue-phase voltage depression
    21% [reported]; duration including voltage recovery 80 ms [reported].
D4  ESO system measurements: voltages recovered to normal less than 100 ms [reported] after the circuit was
    de-energised; the dip was larger at locations near the short circuit, the largest at Wymondley.
D5  Area of the event: harmonics less than 1% [reported]; negative phase sequence (NPS) currents did not
    exceed 0.6% [reported].

SECTION E — OTHER CIRCUIT TRIPS ON 9 AUGUST 2019 (times as printed; clock basis not stated in the sources)
E1  Harker–Stella West 275 kV [reported] circuit. ESO report narrative: at 14:23 [reported] the circuit was
    tripped and automatically returned to service; lightning was observed active in the vicinity; there
    were no adverse effects to the transmission system following this fault. ESO answers to E3C questions
    (Appendix M, Q30): tripped at 14:23:00 [reported]; returned to service via Delayed Auto Reclose (DAR)
    at 14:23:32 [reported].
E2  Blyth–Eccles–Stella West 400 kV [reported] circuit. ESO report narrative: at 16:50:44 [reported] lightning
    struck the circuit near Longframlington, Northumberland; the circuit tripped and closed with no power
    losses associated. ESO answers to E3C questions (Appendix M, Q30), for the Blyth–Eccles–Stella West 1
    400 kV [reported] circuit: tripped at 16:43:25 [reported]; returned to service via DAR at
    16:43:54 [reported]; lightning observed in the vicinity; fault cleared with no adverse effects.

SECTION F — SITE FOLLOW-UP (NGET)
F1  After the event: engineers attended Wymondley Main and Eaton Socon substations to collect data, including
    protection operating data; all assets were operating as normal; no defects identified.
F2  Saturday 10 August 2019, morning: visual inspection of the Eaton Socon–Wymondley Main overhead line; no
    defects observed.

SECTION G — POST-EVENT ASSESSMENTS (attributed later statements; not system records)
G1  NGET report (Appendix C to the ESO technical report of 6 September 2019): the network "operated as
    designed and in line with standards"; main protection cleared the fault within the 80 ms [reported]
    required in the Grid Code; the DAR system operated as expected and designed.
G2  NGET: one of the strikes is timed at the same time as the fault; "As such we can be confident that a
    lightning strike was the cause of the fault."
G3  NGET (power quality analysis and findings): the voltage depressions and durations were as expected for
    this type of fault; electrically further from the fault, voltage dips of 20% [reported] with
    80 ms [reported] duration were observed; the later small transient at Ryhall was most likely associated
    with reactive compensation switching in response to the fault, and was too small to register at Necton.
G4  NGET (steady state, harmonics and NPS): pre-fault and post-fault steady state voltages at Wymondley
    Main, Eaton Socon, Keadby and Killingholme 400 kV [reported] were within the SQSS operational limits of
    ±10% (420 kV to 380 kV) [reported]; harmonics were within the 3% [reported] limit of ER G5/4; NPS
    currents were within the 1.5% [reported] Grid Code limit.
G5  ESO technical report (6 September 2019): all measurements indicate that voltages stayed above the Fault
    Ride Through profile specified in the Grid Code and returned to within steady state limits after the
    event.
G6  ESO technical report: NGET, by analysing its protection data, confirmed that these lightning strikes
    were the cause of the circuit trip and reclose; the transmission system protection operated in line
    with the design and in compliance with the Grid Code requirements on fault clearance.
G7  Ofgem report (3 January 2020): NGET's evidence shows fault clearance times for the two circuit breakers
    under 75 ms [reported] and voltage within a range of 390 kV to 410 kV [reported] following the fault; the
    evidence suggests NGET's transmission assets performed as expected.

DOCUMENT R02 — System conditions data, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: Elexon Limited (BMRS / Insights API data, much of it supplied by the system
operator); National Energy System Operator (NESO) open data portal; National Grid ESO (technical
report tables)
Record type: real public dataset extracts (CSV files) with two published report tables and this
metadata note
STATUS: REAL DATA EXTRACTS WITH TRANSCRIBED REPORT TABLES — dataset values are unchanged from the
publishers' files (only rows and columns were selected); report tables, captions and quotations
are reproduced as printed. Nothing in this record is synthesised.
Clock reference: stated for each file and table below. Elexon timestamps are UTC (ISO-8601 with
Z). Elexon and NESO settlement periods are numbered on the UK local clock: period 1 starts at
00:00 local time and each period lasts 30 minutes. UK local time on 9 August 2019 was BST
(UTC+01:00).
Value-status legend: [measured] metered or observed value as published; [reported] value stated by
its publisher or by a report; [estimated] value its source describes as an estimate; [modelled]
value produced by a model; [digitised] and [illustrative] are not used.

PART A — HOW TO USE THIS RECORD
A1  The CSV files described in Part B are delivered with this note; after retrieval they are in
    $EVIDENCE_DIR/R02/. Dataset values are copied without rounding, unit conversion, interpolation
    or gap filling. CSV conventions for files built from the publishers' JSON: comma-separated,
    UTF-8, LF line endings, one header row; numbers as published; true/false for JSON booleans; an
    empty cell for JSON null. The two NESO files keep the publisher's own lines byte for byte
    (CRLF line endings).
A2  Unit-level metered volumes (B8) and Maximum Export Limit records (B9) are also available
    through query_asset_log for assets HORNSEA-ONE and LITTLE-BARFORD; each row there has an event
    ID and cites R02.
A3  Cite this note with L<n> or L<a>-L<b> (line numbers shown on retrieval).

PART B — PUBLIC DATASET EXTRACTS (one block per file)
B1  File R02_elexon_fuelinst_5min_20190809.csv [measured] — generation outturn by fuel type,
    5-minute values.
    Source: Elexon BMRS dataset FUELINST, Elexon Insights API endpoint /datasets/FUELINST queried
    with publishDateTimeFrom=2019-08-09T14:00:00Z and publishDateTimeTo=2019-08-09T19:00:00Z;
    retrieved 2026-10-20. Publisher: Elexon Limited. Licence: Elexon BMRS open data licence.
    Contains BMRS data (c) Elexon Limited copyright and database right 2026.
    Rows: 61 (every row returned), one per startTime from 2019-08-09T13:55:00Z to
    2019-08-09T18:55:00Z. The API returns one record per fuel type; the file has one column per
    fuel type instead. No totals are added.
    Columns: startTime, publishTime (UTC); settlementDate, settlementPeriod (UK local clock);
    BIOMASS, CCGT, COAL, INTEW, INTFR, INTIRL, INTNED, INTNEM, NPSHYD, NUCLEAR, OCGT, OIL, OTHER,
    PS, WIND (MW). INT* codes are interconnectors; PS is pumped storage; NPSHYD is
    non-pumped-storage hydro (publisher's fuel-type codes).
    Publisher's description: "average MW values over 5 minutes for each category". The data do not
    say whether startTime is the start of the averaging interval, so treat the time of each
    FUELINST value as uncertain by up to 5 minutes. Embedded (distribution-connected) generation
    is not included.
B2  File R02_elexon_fuelhh_halfhour_20190809.csv [measured] — generation outturn by fuel type,
    half-hourly.
    Source: Elexon BMRS dataset FUELHH, endpoint /datasets/FUELHH queried for settlementDate
    2019-08-09; retrieved 2026-10-20. Licence as B1.
    Rows: 48, settlement periods 1-48 of 2019-08-09, in period order. Columns as B1; startTime is
    the UTC start of the settlement period, except that the publisher dates the period-48 row
    2019-08-08T22:30:00Z (kept as published). Publisher's description: "average MW values over 30
    minutes for each category".
    Caveat: on this date the FUELHH value of some settlement periods equals the mean of only the
    first five of the six FUELINST values in that period, not of all six. Do not use FUELHH to
    time changes within a half hour or to check FUELINST.
B3  File R02_elexon_indo_itsdo_20190809.csv [measured] — initial demand outturn, half-hourly.
    Source: Elexon endpoint /demand/outturn queried for settlementDate 2019-08-09; retrieved
    2026-10-20. Licence as B1.
    Rows: 48, settlement periods 1-48. Columns: publishTime, startTime, settlementDate,
    settlementPeriod, initialDemandOutturn, initialTransmissionSystemDemandOutturn. startTime is
    the UTC start of the period and publishTime its end (UTC); values MW.
    Publisher's description: INDO "measures the half-hour average MW demand metered by the
    Transmission Company based on its operational metering"; INDO "takes into account transmission
    losses but does not include station transformer load, pumped storage demand or interconnector
    demand", while ITSDO includes them.
B4  File R02_neso_historic_demand_20190808-10.csv [measured] — NESO historic demand data,
    half-hourly, 8-10 August 2019; its embedded generation columns are [modelled].
    Source: NESO open data portal, Historic Demand Data 2019 (demanddata_2019.csv); retrieved
    2026-10-20. Licence: NESO Open Data Licence v1.0. Supported by National Energy SO Open Data.
    Rows: 144 (48 per day for 08-AUG-2019, 09-AUG-2019 and 10-AUG-2019), copied from the
    publisher's file byte for byte with its header line. Columns: SETTLEMENT_DATE,
    SETTLEMENT_PERIOD, ND, TSD, ENGLAND_WALES_DEMAND, EMBEDDED_WIND_GENERATION,
    EMBEDDED_WIND_CAPACITY, EMBEDDED_SOLAR_GENERATION, EMBEDDED_SOLAR_CAPACITY, NON_BM_STOR,
    PUMP_STORAGE_PUMPING, IFA_FLOW, IFA2_FLOW, BRITNED_FLOW, MOYLE_FLOW, EAST_WEST_FLOW,
    NEMO_FLOW, NSL_FLOW, ELECLINK_FLOW, VIKING_FLOW, GREENLINK_FLOW (MW).
    Publisher's documentation: "All values are an average over the half hour." and "All times are
    UK time and for the half hour beginning." SETTLEMENT_DATE is written DD-MON-YYYY.
    EMBEDDED_WIND_GENERATION and EMBEDDED_SOLAR_GENERATION are model estimates [modelled]: "The
    true output of these generators is not known so an estimate is provided based on NESO's best
    model."
    The publisher's resource record gives created 2020-05-04 and last modified 2025-04-08; the
    copy used here was downloaded on 2026-10-20, and its values may differ from those available in
    2019.
B5  File R02_neso_inertia_20190808-10.csv [modelled] — NESO system inertia estimates, half-hourly,
    8-10 August 2019.
    Source: NESO open data portal, GB System Inertia 2019-2020 (inertia.csv); retrieved
    2026-10-20. Licence as B4.
    Rows: 144 (48 per day), copied byte for byte with the header line. Columns: Settlement Date
    (YYYY-MM-DD), Settlement Period (UK local clock), Outturn Inertia, Market Provided Inertia.
    The file does not state a unit.
    Publisher's resource description: "Estimate of the market provided and outturn inertia for the
    GB Transmission System per settlement period." The resource record gives created 2021-07-01.
B6  File R02_elexon_lolpdrm_20190809.csv [modelled] — loss-of-load probability and de-rated margin
    forecasts.
    Source: Elexon endpoint /forecast/system/loss-of-load (LOLPDRM) for 9 August 2019; retrieved
    2026-10-20. Licence as B1.
    Rows: 240 (settlementDate 2019-08-09, forecast horizons 1, 2, 4, 8 and 12 hours for each of 48
    periods). Columns: publishTime, publishingPeriodCommencingTime, startTime, settlementDate,
    settlementPeriod, forecastHorizon, lossOfLoadProbability, deratedMargin. Times are UTC;
    deratedMargin in MW. For horizons of 1-8 hours "the returned value is the forecast received
    that number of hours before the start of the settlement period". These are forecasts made
    before each period, not outturn.
B7  File R02_elexon_bm_unit_reference.csv [reported] — Elexon BM unit reference data for five
    units.
    Source: Elexon endpoint /reference/bmunits/all; retrieved 2026-10-20. Licence as B1. Rows: 5
    (all fields of the five units listed in C4).
    Caveat: this is the publisher's registration data as served in 2026, not a copy of the
    register in force in August 2019; names and capacities may have changed since.
B8  File R02_elexon_b1610_selected_units_20190809.csv [measured] — metered generation per BM unit
    per settlement period (B1610).
    Source: Elexon endpoint /datasets/B1610/stream, one query per unit for 2019-08-08T23:00:00Z to
    2019-08-09T23:00:00Z; retrieved 2026-10-20. Licence as B1.
    Rows: 192 (units T_HOWAO-1, T_HOWAO-2, T_HOWAO-3, T_LBAR-1; settlementDate 2019-08-09, periods
    1-48; the record for the next settlement date returned by the same query is not included).
    Columns: dataset, psrType, bmUnit, nationalGridBmUnitId, settlementDate, settlementPeriod,
    halfHourEndTime, settlementRunType, quantity.
    quantity is energy in MWh over the settlement period. Publisher: "The generation output
    returned by this endpoint is the metered volume and not the instantaneous power output".
    halfHourEndTime is the UTC end of the period written without a zone designator. Every row has
    settlementRunType DF.
B9  File R02_elexon_mels_selected_units_20190809.csv [reported] — Maximum Export Limit (MEL)
    records for five BM units.
    Source: Elexon endpoint /balancing/physical, one query per unit for 2019-08-08T23:00:00Z to
    2019-08-09T23:00:00Z; retrieved 2026-10-20. Licence as B1.
    Rows: 267 MELS records with settlementDate 2019-08-09 for units T_HOWAO-1, T_HOWAO-2,
    T_HOWAO-3, T_LBAR-1, T_LBAR-1G. Columns: dataset, settlementDate, settlementPeriod, timeFrom,
    timeTo, levelFrom, levelTo, nationalGridBmUnit, bmUnit. Each record is a level from levelFrom

    The same queries returned physical notification (PN) records only for settlement periods 1-4

DOCUMENT R10 — Operating requirements as described in the published reports (selection)
Owner/originator: compiled from the National Grid ESO, Ofgem and E3C reports; no code administrator text
Record type: reconstruction of requirements as the reports describe them, attributed item by item
STATUS: RECONSTRUCTION OF REQUIREMENTS DESCRIBED IN PUBLISHED REPORTS — NOT CODE OR STANDARD TEXT.
The editions of the Grid Code, SQSS and Distribution Code in force on 9 August 2019 have not been
verified for this exercise. Each item restates what the named report says, not the code's own wording.
Clock reference: no clock times are recorded; dates are calendar dates as printed (UK, BST = UTC+01:00).
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in the named report; [measured], [estimated],
[modelled], [digitised] and [illustrative] not used.
Sources: ESO technical report dated 6 September 2019 (ESO), its Appendix H (ESO App. H) and answers to
E3C questions (ESO answers; data available on 28 August 2019); Ofgem report dated 3 January 2020
(Ofgem); E3C interim report, October 2019 (E3C interim); E3C final report, January 2020 (E3C final).

SECTION A — SECURITY STANDARD (SQSS): SECURED EVENTS AND FREQUENCY LIMITS
A1   ESO 2.2: the SQSS specifies the limits of frequency deviations for secured events, which include
     loss of output from a single generating unit, CCGT module, boiler, nuclear reactor or DC bi-pole.
     Normal Infeed Loss Risk: maximum frequency deviation should not exceed 0.5 Hz [reported].
     Infrequent Infeed Loss Risk: frequency should not deviate outside the range 49.5 Hz [reported]
     to 50.5 Hz [reported] for more than 60 seconds [reported].
A2   ESO 2.2: the level of the normal infeed loss actually covered depends on the configuration of the
     system at the time (printed as "typically it is c. 1,000W" [reported]); the current normal
     infrequent infeed maximum loss risk is 1,260 MW [reported] for when Sizewell is at full load.
A3   ESO App. H: 'Normal Infeed Loss' is the maximum loss the system should be able to manage without
     the frequency going below 49.5 Hz [reported] (e.g. an interconnector at 1,000 MW [reported]);
     'Infrequent Infeed Loss' is a higher level (e.g. Sizewell at 1,260 MW [reported]) for which the
     frequency should not go below 49.2 Hz [reported] and should recover to 49.5 Hz [reported] within
     one minute.
A4   ESO App. H: the SQSS anticipates only one Secured Event at any one time and does not assume
     multiple Secured Events occurring simultaneously (N-1). The Power Infeed Loss is the power infeed
     that can be lost in one Secured Event: generally a single large generator, or two or more smaller
     generators connected through an asset treated as a single Secured Event (for example a double
     circuit overhead line or busbar).
A5   ESO App. H: the system should be re-secured as soon as reasonably practicable after the occurrence
     of a Secured Event.
A6   ESO glossary: "The current maximum upper limit for an infrequent infeed loss risk is 1800MW." [reported]
A7   Ofgem Box 4: the SQSS requires frequency to stay above or equal to 49.5 Hz [reported], or any fall
     below that level to be recovered within 60 seconds [reported], for such events; the ESO is required
     to secure the system by holding reserves so that the frequency limits are not breached.
A8   E3C final, footnote 14: the SQSS allows a deviation below 49.5 Hz [reported] provided that the
     frequency is returned to 49.5 Hz [reported] within 60 seconds [reported].
A9   Ofgem 3.2 and 3.5: the ESO does not consider it is required to secure against distributed generation
     losses under the SQSS; it follows an internal policy of securing against both transmission-connected
     and vector shift distributed generation losses for credible transmission faults during periods of
     increased risk (e.g. bad weather, lightning) or when it considers it economic to do so.

SECTION B — LARGEST LOSS, RATE OF CHANGE OF FREQUENCY AND VECTOR SHIFT (as ESO describes its practice)
B1   ESO App. H: in securing for the largest loss the ESO takes into account the protection setting
     historically specified in the Distribution Code for RoCoF of 0.125 Hz/s [reported], and seeks to
     ensure the system is configured in real time so that this limit is not breached for an infeed loss.
B2   ESO answer 11: the ESO secures the system to within a RoCoF limit of 0.125 Hz/s [reported] for the
     largest credible loss, and schedules frequency response so that the largest loss is contained to
     49.5 Hz [reported] for a normal loss and 49.2 Hz [reported] for an abnormal loss.
B3   ESO App. H: approximately 2 GW [reported] of small generators are connected to the distribution
     networks via relays which disconnect them if the RoCoF is greater than 0.125 Hz/s [reported].
B4   ESO App. H: approximately 8.5 GW [reported] of small generators are connected via relays which
     disconnect them if the vector shift angle is greater than 6 degrees [reported].
B5   ESO App. H: vector shift risks are divided into Type A (transmission faults with no coincident loss
     of BMU infeed, e.g. an overhead line) and Type B (transmission faults with coincident loss of BMU
     infeed, e.g. a generator busbar). The largest Type A risk is monitored for each half-hourly
     settlement period; Type B faults are only secured where it is economic to do so.

SECTION C — FREQUENCY RESPONSE AND RESERVE PRODUCTS (definitions as ESO describes them)
C1   ESO App. H: primary response must be delivering its required output by 10 seconds [reported]
     following the trip and continue for a further 20 seconds [reported] (30 seconds total).
C2   ESO App. H: secondary response must be delivering its required output by 30 seconds [reported]
     following the change in frequency and continue for a further 30 minutes [reported].
C3   ESO App. H: dynamic response is a continuously provided service to manage normal fluctuations in the
     frequency; static response is provided when the system frequency transgresses the low frequency
     relay setting on site. Both can come from generation and demand, BM and non-BM units.
C4   ESO App. H: Mandatory Frequency Response (MFR) can only be provided by synchronised BM units and is
     an obligation of the Grid Code; commercial response is procured from generation or demand, BM or
     non-BM units, whose providers are required to deliver the contracted amount.
C5   ESO answer 13: Firm Frequency Response (FFR) is tendered for on a monthly basis; Mandatory Frequency
     Response has similar characteristics but is an obligation in a generator's connection agreement;
     Enhanced Frequency Response (EFR) is a faster form of FFR; static frequency response reduces demand
     or increases generation when the frequency hits a trigger limit.
C6   ESO answer 13: reserve services: Short Term Operating Reserve typically delivers energy
     within 20 minutes [reported] or less; Rapid Start provides access to energy in less than
     2 minutes [reported]; Balancing Mechanism actions.
C7   ESO App. H: a minimum amount of dynamic response must be held for steady state frequency control;
     the minimum dynamic response requirement at the time of the incident was set to 550 MW [reported].

SECTION D — LOW FREQUENCY DEMAND DISCONNECTION (LFDD)
D1   ESO 4.3: the Grid Code requires each DNO to make arrangements that will enable automatic
     disconnection of demand if the frequency on the transmission system drops below
     48.8 Hz [reported]; demand is disconnected in staged blocks (5%, 7.5% and 10%) [reported].
D2   E3C final, Table 1 "Low Frequency Demand Disconnection settings for each frequency disconnection
     stages" (% of demand disconnection in each transmission area; an area is listed only where the
     table prints a value): E&W = England & Wales (NGET); SPT = Southern Scotland; SHET = Northern Scotland
     Stage 1 | 48.80 Hz [reported] | E&W 5 [reported]
     Stage 2 | 48.75 Hz [reported] | E&W 5 [reported]
     Stage 3 | 48.70 Hz [reported] | E&W 10 [reported]
     Stage 4 | 48.60 Hz [reported] | E&W 7.5 [reported] | SHET 10 [reported]
     Stage 5 | 48.50 Hz [reported] | E&W 7.5 [reported] | SPT 10 [reported]
     Stage 6 | 48.40 Hz [reported] | E&W 7.5 [reported] | SPT 10 [reported] | SHET 10 [reported]
     Stage 7 | 48.20 Hz [reported] | E&W 7.5 [reported] | SPT 10 [reported] | SHET 10 [reported]
     Stage 8 | 48.00 Hz [reported] | E&W 5 [reported] | SPT 10 [reported] | SHET 10 [reported]
     Stage 9 | 47.80 Hz [reported] | E&W 5 [reported]
     Total % demand | E&W 60 [reported] | SPT 40 [reported] | SHET 40 [reported]
D3   Ofgem 3.38: Grid Code Operating Code 6 requires each DNO in England and Wales to have LFDD equipment
     in place to disconnect a maximum of 60% [reported] of demand (measured at winter demand), operating
     in stages; the requirements contain an accuracy tolerance for the frequency levels and a time delay
     permitted for different LFDD equipment, depending on its installation date.
D4   Ofgem 3.39: Stage 1 of the LFDD required 5% [reported] of winter peak demand to be disconnected.
D5   E3C final, on the 5% [reported] figure: "The 5% demand figure is based on forecasted peak demand
     during an average cold spell."
D6   E3C interim: the scheme is designed to disconnect between 5 - 60% [reported] of total peak demand
     through 9 [reported] stages as the system frequency reaches certain trigger levels.
D7   ESO glossary: LFDD is set up in agreement with the ESO by DNOs to reduce their demand in
     5% [reported] stages of total demand (printed as "up to 40% available") [reported].
D8   Ofgem 3.44: SP Distribution, being part of the SP Transmission network area, is not required by the
     Grid Code to disconnect demand until frequency reaches 48.5 Hz [reported].
D9   ESO 2.5: Grid Code OC6.6 describes the automatic LFDD scheme and the arrangements the DNOs are
     required to make in relation to it; following operation of the scheme, the DNOs must notify ESO of
     its operation and are not permitted to restore automatically disconnected demand without
     instruction from National Grid ESO.
D10  Ofgem 3.40: the Grid Code does not currently regulate the disconnection of distributed generation
     through LFDD.

SECTION E — DISTRIBUTED GENERATION PROTECTION (Distribution Code, as the reports describe it)
E1   E3C final: under the Distribution Code, embedded generators are required to install protection
     which detects when the generator is islanded and safely shuts the plant down, predominantly by
     monitoring the rate of change of frequency or the change in voltage phase angle (vector shift).
E2   E3C final: requirements introduced in 2014 [reported] required all generators with a capacity
     greater than 5 MW [reported] to install RoCoF protection with specific settings; this was
     implemented across all relevant sites in 2018 [reported], and the Accelerated Loss of Mains
     Protection programme was initiated in 2019 [reported] for embedded generators between
     5 MW and 50 kW [reported].
E3   Ofgem, footnote 18: vector shift protection is no longer permitted for distributed generators
     connected after 1 February 2018 [reported].
E4   Ofgem 3.32: Distribution Code changes reduced the frequency level triggering under frequency
     protections to 47 Hz [reported], permitted for distributed generators with capacities greater
     than 5 MW [reported] from August 2010 [reported].

DOCUMENT S12 — Engineering analysis records, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: National Grid ESO (analysis and modelling), with Ofgem and E3C analysis as attributed
Record type: reconstructed register of published analysis records, each attributed to its source and date
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: times are as printed by the sources, which label no clock; read as BST (UTC+01:00)
because ESO dates the event at 4:52pm. Inertia values are written in the unit each source prints.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated by the source; [estimated] value the source calls an
estimate or approximation; [modelled] value the source derives from simulation or a model;
[measured], [digitised] and [illustrative] not used.
Sources: ESO technical report dated 6 September 2019 (with appendices); ESO answers to E3C questions
(appendix M; ESO states these use the data available to it on 28 August 2019); Ofgem report dated
3 January 2020; E3C interim report (October 2019); E3C final report (January 2020).

SECTION A — ACCOUNTING OF GENERATION LOST (each total keeps its source's components and stage)
A1   ESO technical report, Table 2 "Table of cumulative infeed losses" (unit: infeed loss | cumulative):
     Little Barford ST1C 244 MW [reported] | 244 MW [reported]
     Hornsea Offshore Windfarm 737 MW [reported] | 981 MW [reported]
     Estimated, embedded generation infeed loss due to Vector Shift Loss of Mains Protection
       150 MW [estimated] | 1,131 MW [reported]
     Estimated, embedded generation infeed loss due to RoCoF Loss of Mains Protection
       350 MW [estimated] | 1,481 MW [reported]
     Little Barford GT1A 210 MW [reported] | 1,691 MW [reported]
     Little Barford GT1B 187 MW [reported] | 1,878 MW [reported]
A2   ESO technical report, section 3.2, footnote 1: the second gas turbine at Little Barford tripped from
     187 MW [reported] after the initiation of LFDD, bringing total generation lost through the event to
     1,878 MW [reported]; its effect was absorbed by the action of LFDD and additional plant dispatched
     by the ENCC.
A3   ESO technical report, Appendix H: the events are considered as three separate (albeit
     simultaneous) Secured Events: the loss of Hornsea (737 MW [reported]), the loss of Little Barford
     (641 MW [reported]) and the loss of vector shift generation (150 MW [estimated]); the total of
     1528 MW [reported] was significantly in excess of the level secured for (1,000 MW [reported]).
     In addition, approximately 350 MW [estimated] of embedded generation tripped on RoCoF protection.
A4   Ofgem 2.4.5: the events resulted in a cumulative power loss of more than 1,130 MW [reported] within
     around 1 second [reported] of the fault.
A5   Ofgem 2.4.7: after the RoCoF trips described in 2.4.6, "The cumulative loss of generation at
     this point was around 1,500MW" [estimated]; the ESO held sufficient frequency response and reserve
     for a 1,000 MW [reported] generation loss.
A6   Ofgem 2.4.10-2.4.11 and footnote 20: after one of the Little Barford gas turbines
     (210 MW [reported]) and a further net reduction in generation of 200 MW [reported] at 49 Hz,
     "The cumulative loss of generation at this point was at least 1,990MW" [reported]; the 200 MW
     figure is net of demand disconnection, such as trains and large industrial customers.
A7   E3C interim report: the total generation lost from the affected power stations, as part of the
     initial event, was in the region of 2,100 MW [estimated], greater than the response held.
A8   E3C final report: the total generation lost from the affected power stations and a number of
     smaller generators, as part of the initial event, was at least 2,000 MW [reported].

SECTION B — FREQUENCY SIMULATION OF THE EVENT (ESO technical report, Appendix I)
B1   The Frequency Simulation Engine (FSE) was used to infer the imbalance between supply and demand that
     would produce the actual frequency curve; the output of the frequency response services was then
     removed, leaving the changes in underlying supply and demand required to obtain the trace.
B2   ESO: "An event such as this is complex with many different things happening and so it is unlikely
     that we can explain all of the movements in the imbalance."
B3   Appendix I, Table 1 "Modelled Imbalance Time Series" (columns: event | time | imbalance change); every
     row is an input of the simulation and is tagged as such:
     Hornsea One | 16:52:33.728 | -737 MW [modelled]
     Little Barford ST1C | 16:52:34 | -244 MW [modelled]
     Loss of Mains – Vector Shift | 16:52:34 | -150 MW [modelled]
     Loss of Mains - RoCoF | 16:52:34 | -430 MW [modelled]
     Reduction in generator output over 30 seconds | 16:53:10 | -100 MW [modelled]
     Little Barford GT1A | 16:53:30 | -210 MW [modelled]
     Net Change due to protection at 49.0 Hz | 16:53:40* | -200 MW [modelled]
     Net demand change at 48.8 Hz | 16:53:48* | +350 MW [modelled]
     Little Barford GT1B | 16:53:58 | -187 MW [modelled]
     The source marks two times with an asterisk and does not define the mark.
B4   Appendix I: a 100 MW [modelled] variation in underlying imbalance, which can be attributed to a
     slight reduction in generation output across the fleet lasting for 30 seconds [modelled], is
     modelled during the return of the frequency.
B5   ESO technical report, section 4.4 and Appendix I: the simulation maps closely to the actual
     (smoothed) frequency trace; modelling inputs complete at 16:54 [reported], hence the deviation of
     the trace from that point onwards.
B6   ESO technical report, section 4.4: two simulations of a 1,000 MW [modelled] loss with the same
     inertia and demand (full contracted response; actual delivered response) both keep frequency above
     49.5 Hz [modelled].

SECTION C — RECORDS OF A CHANGE OF ABOUT 100 MW, BY SOURCE (each as its source states it)
C1   Ofgem 2.4.9: there was a reduction in frequency equivalent to a 100 MW [reported] reduction in
     generation or increase in demand over 30 seconds [reported]. The ESO has stated that during this
     time there were a number of movements in both demand and generation but it is unable to precisely
     point to the source of change.
C2   ESO Appendix I (see B4): modelled as a slight reduction in generation output across the fleet.
C3   E3C final report: the ESO technical report identified that an unexpected increase in electricity
     demand occurred in parallel with the loss of generation; this has been attributed to the de-loading
     or tripping of 100 MW [reported] of embedded generation, but the cause for this loss is unknown at
     present.

SECTION D — RESPONSE PLANNING ASSUMPTIONS AND DELIVERY ASSESSMENTS
D1   ESO Appendix H: the FSE adopts a pessimistic approach: the starting frequency is set as
     49.9 Hz [reported] for low frequency response calculation (in real time it would generally be
     kept higher), and response services are modelled at their minimum performance requirement.
D2   ESO answer 18 (data available on 28 August 2019): when calculating the volume of frequency response
     required to secure the largest loss, a 90% [reported] delivery rate is assumed.
D3   ESO answer 17, table note: demand varies with frequency; for 29 GW [reported] demand this effect is
     approximately 350 MW [estimated] at 49.5 Hz [reported], and it is unrelated to LFDD.
D4   ESO technical report, section 4.4: conservative modelling assumptions are employed to ensure there
     is contingency if not all contracted response delivers; overall response performance on 9 August
     was broadly in line with these planning assumptions, with some under-performance being followed up.
D5   ESO answer 27: in the days immediately after the event the ESO held 100 MW [reported] more frequency
     response whilst it analysed the incident, and has since removed this extra holding.
D6   Ofgem 3.6: there was only a narrow margin for error in securing the system against
     transmission-connected generator losses alone, and a high level of sensitivity to small changes in
     key assumptions; the ESO's processes for estimating the impact of distributed generation on
     requirements do not appear sufficiently robust.
D7   Ofgem 3.9: primary response providers under-delivered by 17% [reported] and secondary response
     providers by 14% [reported]; mandatory response providers, and commercial Fast Frequency Response
     providers of dynamic primary response (Ofgem's wording), under-delivered by approximately
     25% [reported].
D8   Ofgem 3.12: Ofgem does not believe that better response and reserve delivery would have been
     sufficient to prevent demand from being disconnected for this event.

SECTION E — INERTIA FIGURES AND ASSUMPTIONS
E1   ESO technical report, Table 4 (comparison of system conditions, 1 July and 9 August): inertia
     201 GVAs [reported] on 1 July and 210GVAs [reported] on 9 August.
E2   ESO answer 42 (data available on 28 August 2019): the ESO does not currently measure system inertia
     directly but estimates it using a model, derived from the forecasted demand level, embedded solar
     and wind. Estimated inertia (MVA.s) by timestamp and system condition:
     11:00 [reported], 6 hours before the incident: 201353 [estimated]
     16:52 [reported], immediately prior to the trip: 219632 [estimated]
     16:52:34 [reported], LBAR ST1 trip and 500MW embedded generation loss: 216885 [estimated]
     16:52:58 [reported], LFGT service kicked in: 218013 [estimated]
     16:53:31 [reported], LBAR GT1A trip: 216177 [estimated]
     16:53:49 [reported], LFDD operated, 931MW drop reported from DNOs: 214222 [estimated]
     16:53:58 [reported], LBAR GT1B trip: 212386 [estimated]
     16:57 [reported], frequency restored with additional units on: 215356 [estimated]
E3   ESO Appendix H: to increase the inertia of the system to allow 1 MW [reported] more of infeed loss
     generally requires adding 20 MW [reported] of synchronous generation to the system.
E4   Ofgem 3.8: the ESO used 8 [reported] sample events in 2016/17 (when demand and system inertia was
     higher) to build its model of the contribution of demand response to system inertia, which it
     validates against actual system events.

SECTION F — ESO EARLIER ACCOUNT (ANSWERS TO E3C, DATA AT 28 AUGUST 2019) AND FINAL REPORT (6 SEPTEMBER)
F1   Embedded generation. Earlier (answer 7): approximately 500 MW [estimated] lost, split between RoCoF
     and vector shift not yet determined. Final report (section 4.2): approximately 150 MW [estimated]
     on vector shift and approximately 350 MW [estimated] on RoCoF.
F2   Loss of mains volume. Earlier (answers 2 and 3): "the loss was in line with our forecasts for such an
     event". Final report (section 7): levels "were broadly in line with what was expected".
F3   LFDD. Earlier (answer 31): "Initial analysis for the Interim Report suggests that the LFDD worked as
     intended." Final report (section 4.3): "The LFDD process worked largely as expected", having provided
     slightly lower than 5% [reported] of demand.
F4   Restoration. Earlier (answers 2 and 3): system returned to a stable position in
     c. 15 minutes [reported]; DNOs then restored supplies in c. 30 minutes [reported]. Final report
     (section 3.2):
     DNOs restored supplies within 40 minutes [reported] once the system was stable and secure.
F5   Secondary response holding at the event time. Earlier (answer 16, table): 1338 MW [reported] total
     low frequency secondary holding at 16:52 [reported]. Final report (Table 3): 1314 MW [reported].
F6   Inertia before the event. Earlier (answer 42): 219632 MVA.s [estimated] immediately prior to the
     trip. Final report (Table 4): 210GVAs [reported].
F7   Little Barford GT1A. Final report, executive summary: the gas turbine trip at 210 MW [reported] was
     "due to high pressure in the steam bypass system following the failure of a bypass valve to operate
     correctly". Same report, section 4.2: RWE confirmed that "for reasons presently unknown", after
     approximately 1 minute [reported], the first gas turbine tripped "due to a high-pressure excursion
     in the steam bypass system".

DOCUMENT S01 — Hornsea One offshore wind farm event log, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: Ørsted (Hornsea One operator)
Record type: plant configuration note, event log extract and separately dated post-event annotations
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: this reconstructed log is rendered in UTC with an explicit Z suffix. The operator's
published timeline uses local time (16:52:33:490, 16:52:33:728) except one passage, written 15.52.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in the operator's published material or in published
accounts of it; [estimated] approximate value derived from a reported description; [measured] and
[illustrative] not used. "~" marks a value the source gives as approximate.

PART 1 — PLANT CONFIGURATION ON 9 AUGUST 2019
P1  Hornsea One: offshore wind farm 120 km [reported] from the Yorkshire coast, under construction offshore;
    1.2 GW [reported] installed capacity when complete (174 [reported] turbines rated 7 MW [reported]).
P2  Three phases of 400 MW [reported] each: Hornsea 1A, Hornsea 1B and Hornsea 1C. Each phase connects to its
    own HVAC collector substation, then an offshore HVAC reactive compensation station, an onshore HVAC
    substation and the National Grid 400 kV [reported] substation at Killingholme.
P3  Two modules fully installed and the third partially installed: declared export capability
    800 MW [reported].
P4  Internal network outage configuration: one SGT and one offshore transmission system user asset (OTSUA)
    circuit on outage.
P5  Hornsea 1B (circuit Z12) operating at 400 MW [reported] before the event (maximum for that unit).

PART 2 — EVENT LOG (raw entries; times UTC, explicit Z)
Time (UTC) and status           Entry
~15:42Z [estimated]             Reactive power output response to a 2% [reported] voltage step change. See

C3  Modelling with the equipment manufacturer before 9 August suggested voltage control performance issues at

PART 1 — SHIFT NARRATIVE (reconstructed from published accounts)
Plant state before the disturbance
N1  The station (740 MW [reported] CCGT, connected at Eaton Socon 400 kV [reported] substation) had
    all three units operating: gas turbines GT1A and GT1B and steam turbine ST1C.
Steam turbine trip
N2  At the start of the station's event sequence the 110 V AC UPS -B- and then UPS -A- raised general
    fault alarms (station sequence-of-events record).
N3  Within 1 second [reported] of the lightning strike and the resulting transmission system disturbance,
    steam turbine ST1C tripped while generating 244 MW [reported].
Steam bypass operation
N4  With the steam turbine lost, the plant went into steam bypass mode: steam generated from the gas
    turbines is fed directly into the condenser. This is the normal operation following loss of the
    steam turbine, intended to allow sustained operation of the gas turbines.
N5  Following the steam turbine trip, the pressure in the steam system rose.
First gas turbine trip
N6  Around a minute [reported] after the transmission system fault, gas turbine GT1A (generating
    210 MW [reported]) tripped automatically due to a high-pressure excursion in the steam bypass system.
Second gas turbine trip
N7  The steam system pressure continued to rise after the GT1A trip, and the plant operators made the
    decision to manually trip the other operational gas turbine due to safety risks.
N8  Around 30 seconds [reported] after the GT1A trip, GT1B (187 MW [reported]) was manually tripped by
    the operating staff in response to high steam pressures. Total station loss: 641 MW [reported].

dated 30 August 2019:
A1  UPS: "The investigation to date has found that all UPS' at Site have functioned correctly to enable
    continuity of supply to plant equipment." "Therefore, we do not now believe the UPS' were related
    to the subsequent trip."

    consequence of the system disturbance. The exact characteristic of the power supply to the UPS
    causing it to switch to battery operation is still to be determined and subject to further
    investigation."
A3  UPS: OEM resilience testing requested during the outage commencing 6 September 2019 [reported].
A4  Steam turbine: "Our investigations have confirmed that the Steam Turbine tripped due to a
    discrepancy in the speed signals after the point of the Transmission System fault clearance."
    A comprehensive investigation of hardware, software, fault handling and diagnostic coverage for
    the conditions the steam turbine was subjected to during this rare system disturbance is ongoing.
A5  Gas turbines: "For reasons presently unknown a high-pressure excursion occurred on GT1A resulting in
    an automated trip. Given the prevailing conditions all systems functioned as expected. GT1B was
    manually tripped shortly after as a result of excessive steam pressure."
A6  Gas turbines: "A physical inspection of the bypass system is now planned during the forthcoming
    outage in September 2019 to help determine the root cause of the pressure excursions."

B1  3.28: "We have established that the steam turbine tripped initially because of a discrepancy in the
    three [reported] independent speed sensors on the turbine. This discrepancy exceeded the tolerance
    of the control system, causing the generator to automatically shut down. The root cause of the

DOCUMENT R05 — Hornsea One voltage and power traces digitised from published charts, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: National Grid ESO (published report charts; Appendix D charts supplied by Ørsted)
Record type: digitised time series (four CSV files), a calibration file and this method note
STATUS: DIGITISED FROM PUBLISHED CHARTS — NOT ORIGINAL MEASUREMENT DATA. Values were read from chart images in
published reports; they are no more precise than the charts and every value carries an uncertainty.
Clock reference: times are given as printed on each chart's time axis; no chart prints a time zone.
The time_bst_iso column appends +01:00 (BST = UTC+01:00) to the printed time; see CLOCK BASIS.
Value-status legend: [digitised] value read from a published chart by the method below; [reported]
value stated in the text of a published report. Tick values, pixel sizes and fit residuals are
calibration metadata and are not tagged.

SOURCES AND LICENCE
ESO: National Grid ESO, Technical Report on the events of 9 August 2019 (published 6 September 2019), PDF page
19 (printed page 20): Figure 7 'Voltage and Active Power at Hornsea' and Figure 8 'Voltage and Reactive Power
at Hornsea', section 4.2 Generation Performance.
APP: Appendices to that report, Appendix D (Ørsted Technical Report for National Grid ESO, dated 5 September
2019), PDF page 40 Figure 3 and PDF page 41 Figure 4.
Licence: neither document states an open licence. The PDFs and chart images are not part of this record; only
values read from the charts are given, with attribution.

FILES (delivered with this document; after retrieval in $EVIDENCE_DIR/R05/)
app_p40_fig3_onshore.csv: APP p40 Figure 3, 335 data rows, 5 series.
app_p41_fig4_offshore_1b.csv: APP p41 Figure 4, 395 data rows, 5 series.
eso_p19_fig7_voltage_active_power.csv: ESO p19 Figure 7, 594 data rows, 2 series.
eso_p19_fig8_reactive_power.csv: ESO p19 Figure 8, 296 data rows, 1 series.
calibration.json: per chart, the axis ticks used, fitted pixel-to-value maps and residuals,
the series colours and stroke widths, and the uncertainty terms.

CSV COLUMNS (UTF-8, comma-separated, LF line endings, one header row, long format)
time_as_printed: the time on the chart's own time scale, in the chart's own format (see SERIES).
time_bst_iso: time_as_printed as ISO-8601 with +01:00 appended; empty where the axis does not print
  an absolute time for each sample (APP Figure 3).
value, unit: the digitised value [digitised] and its unit (kV, MW or MVAr).
uncertainty: half-width of the plausible range of value at that time, same unit (see UNCERTAINTY).
series_id: <chart id>/<legend name as printed, spaces replaced by underscores>.
sample_index: category index (APP charts: 0 = first plotted sample) or resampling index (ESO charts).
time_uncertainty_s: uncertainty of the printed time scale itself, in seconds (see CLOCK BASIS).
flags: empty, or ';'-separated: ambiguous_overlap (stroke overlaps others of similar colour; the
  uncertainty includes this), at_axis_top / at_axis_bottom (stroke touches the plot edge, so the
  plotted value may be clipped).

SERIES
APP p40 Figure 3 (Ørsted), title as printed 'Hornsea - 16:52, 9th August 2019', caption 'Figure 3 – Showing
Voltage, Active power (MW) and Reactive power (MVAr) from Hornsea One at the time of the de-load'. The report
text says it shows the NETS voltage in the 400kV substation [reported]. Five traces: HOW V1, HOW V2, HOW V3
(voltage, left axis 'Voltage (kV)'; phase or line quantity not stated), HOW active MW and HOW reactive MVAr
(right axis titled 'Reactive power (MVArs)', used for both). 70 plotted samples on a category axis labelled to
0.1 s ('52:33.0' ... '52:34.3', five samples per label); file app_p40_fig3_onshore.csv.
APP p41 Figure 4 (Ørsted), title as printed 'Hornsea 1B - De-load event, voltage vs MW vs MVAr', caption
'Figure 4 – The de-load of Hornsea 1B due to overcurrent at the WTGs'. The report text says it depicts the
offshore conditions at Hornsea 1B (circuit Z12) [reported]. Digitised: kV_PPM1_AVE ... kV_PPM4_AVE (34 kV
collection-system voltage per PPM, left axis 'Voltage (kV)') and MW_OFS (right axis 'Active and Reactive Power
(MW/MVAr)'; the abbreviation is not defined in the report). 79 plotted samples, each labelled with a time to
the millisecond ('16:52:33.211' ... '16:52:33.999', spacing 9-11 ms); file app_p41_fig4_offshore_1b.csv.
ESO p19 Figure 7 'Voltage and Active Power at Hornsea' and Figure 8 'Voltage and Reactive Power at Hornsea'.
The ESO text describes the reaction 'as seen at the onshore connection point' [reported]. Figure 7: Hornsea
Voltage (left axis 'Voltage (kV)') and Total Active Power (right axis 'Active Power (MW)'); Figure 8: Total
Reactive Power (right axis printed 'Rective Power (MVAr)'). Continuous time axes with ticks every 0.25 s
('16:52:33.25' ... '16:52:34.25'); the logger's sample interval is not visible. Resampled every 5 ms from
16:52:33.005 to 16:52:34.485 (axis readings); files eso_p19_fig7_voltage_active_power.csv and
eso_p19_fig8_reactive_power.csv.

METHOD
1. Each chart's embedded raster image was extracted losslessly from the PDF with PyMuPDF at its native
resolution (APP Figure 3 about 196 dpi, Figure 4 about 223 dpi, ESO Figure 7 about 150 dpi, Figure 8 about 96
dpi on the page). A MuPDF render of the same page region agrees with the raster apart from resampling at line
edges, so nothing else on the page (clip paths, vector drawings) alters the chart. Rendering at a higher
resolution only interpolates these pixels and adds no information.
2. Axes were calibrated from their printed ticks: tick positions measured in the image (gridlines, or the
centres of the tick labels where the axis has no gridlines), tick values as printed, and a least-squares
straight line fitted per axis (at least five ticks per axis; residuals under CALIBRATION).
3. Curves were extracted by colour. Each series' colour and stroke width were measured from its legend swatch.
Call-out boxes, arrows and dashed lines (drawn on top of the charts) were masked; gridlines were modelled as
background. The chart was then re-drawn from candidate vertex positions with every series in legend order
(later series on top) and the positions chosen that best reproduce the image: dynamic programming over stroke
positions found in the image, then refinement to 0.05 px. For the APP charts the vertices are the plotted
samples; for the ESO charts one vertex per pixel column, resampled every 5 ms (about one stroke width).
4. Checks: the digitised values were drawn back onto the source images and inspected; ESO Figure 7 and Figure
8 voltages (the same quantity) were digitised independently and agree. No digitised value was adjusted to
agree with any value stated in a report's text.

CALIBRATION (rms residual of the straight-line fit through the printed ticks)
APP p40 Figure 3: left 8 ticks, 0.1218 kV/px, rms 0.025 kV; right 22 ticks, 3.66 MW/MVAr/px, rms 1.2 MW/MVAr;
x 70 labels, 15.10 px/sample, rms 0.09 px.
APP p41 Figure 4: left 9 ticks, 0.06448 kV/px, rms 0.025 kV; right 12 ticks, 0.887 MW/MVAr/px, rms 0.38
MW/MVAr; x 79 labels, 16.29 px/sample, rms 0.27 px.
ESO p19 Figure 7: left 9 ticks, 0.2532 kV/px, rms 0.063 kV; right 10 ticks, 2.85 MW/px, rms 0.73 MW; time 5
ticks, 1.87 ms/px, rms 0.46 ms.
ESO p19 Figure 8: left 9 ticks, 0.3954 kV/px, rms 0.065 kV; right 10 ticks, 8.9 MVAr/px, rms 3.5 MVAr; time 5
ticks, 2.94 ms/px, rms 0.03 ms.

UNCERTAINTY
The uncertainty column combines in quadrature, in pixels converted to the series' unit: the axis fit's rms
residual; half the stroke width (the plotted value lies somewhere within the drawn line); colour ambiguity
(the half-width of the range of positions that reproduce the image about as well as the chosen one: small for
a clearly visible stroke, large where strokes of similar colour overlap or an annotation hides the line); and
the local slope times the time-axis fit residual. It does not include the uncertainty of the time scale itself
(time_uncertainty_s) or any error in the original measurement.
APP p40 Figure 3: kV median 0.2, max 1.3; MW median 5.8, max 9.8; MVAr median 5.8, max 12.
APP p41 Figure 4: kV median 0.17, max 0.43; MW median 1.6, max 3.8.
ESO p19 Figure 7: kV median 0.41, max 1.5; MW median 4.6, max 42.
ESO p19 Figure 8: MVAr median 10, max 32.

CLOCK BASIS
No chart prints a time zone, and no chart states which recorder or clock produced its time scale or how that
clock was synchronised. APP Figure 3 prints only minutes, seconds and tenths ('52:33.0'); the hour comes from
its title ('16:52'). Five consecutive samples share each label, so a sample's time is known only to about 0.1
s from its label; the labels do not say whether they are truncated or rounded. The spacing of about 20 ms per
sample is an inference from five samples per 0.1 s label, not printed. time_bst_iso is left empty for this
chart.
APP Figure 4 prints a time to the millisecond for every sample, with hour 16.
ESO Figures 7 and 8 print tick labels to 0.01 s, with hour 16; times between ticks are read from the fitted
scale. In time_bst_iso the printed hour is read as BST; this is an interpretation, not a statement on the
charts.

NOT DIGITISED
APP Figure 3, HOW reactive MVAr samples 4-18: hidden behind the border of a call-out box drawn on the chart;
omitted from the CSV.
APP p41 Figure 4, MVAr_PPM1, MVAr_PPM2, MVAr_PPM3, MVAr_PPM4: The four per-PPM reactive-power traces lie
within a few pixels of each other for most of the event, MVAr_PPM1 and MVAr_PPM4 are drawn in the same colour,
and repeated fits did not assign the overlapping strokes to the same series consistently (QA overlays showed
strokes swapped between series after the de-load). They are not digitised rather than guessed.
ESO p19 Figure 8, Hornsea Voltage: Same quantity as the voltage in ESO p19 Figure 7, drawn at lower
resolution; digitised only to cross-check the two charts' axes, not written out.

CITING THIS RECORD
This note: L<n> or L<a>-L<b> using the line numbers shown when the document is retrieved.
Summary readings from these series are also available as HORNSEA-ONE asset-log rows (evidence R05),
cited as event:<event_id>. CSV values: cite the line of this note that describes the series and give
the file, series_id and time_as_printed in the finding.

DOCUMENT S06 — Embedded generation returns and published loss estimates, 9 August 2019
Owner/originator: Distribution Network Operators (returns to ESO); estimates by National Grid ESO, Ofgem
and the E3C as attributed below
Record type: reconstructed summary of the DNO embedded-generation return, its stated limits, and
published loss estimates listed by source, each with the source's own timing or stage words
STATUS: SYNTHESISED FOR EVALUATION — NOT REAL EVIDENCE. Reconstructed from published investigation
material for this exercise; wording, layout and record structure are reconstructions.
Clock reference: times are hh:mm:ss as printed by ESO, with no clock labelled; read as BST (UTC+01:00)
because ESO dates the event at 4:52pm.
Value-status legend: [reported] value as stated in a return or report; [estimated] value the source
calls an estimate or approximation; [modelled] value the source derives from frequency simulation or
modelling; [measured], [digitised] and [illustrative] not used.
No estimate below is a direct measurement of embedded generation output; each states its own basis.

PART 1 — DNO RETURNS TO THE ESO DATA REQUEST (as described in the ESO technical report dated
6 September 2019, section 4.2)
R1   After the event ESO contacted all DNOs and requested data on the volume of embedded generation that
     was disconnected or changed output during the event, and asked them to indicate the reason for the
     change of output, for example RoCoF, Vector Shift or Active Network Management (ANM) operation.
R2   All DNOs responded and indicated a combined total of 462 MW [reported] of embedded generation lost
     during the event.
R3   Some DNOs noted challenges in obtaining the data due to the way it is collected or stored. Without
     confirmation from generators, DNOs were unable to determine whether a specific generator tripped due
     to RoCoF or Vector Shift.
R4   A number of embedded generators and demand customers advised that their protection operated when
     the frequency reached 49 Hz [reported] and as such they were disconnected from the system.

PART 2 — LIMITS OF THE AVAILABLE DATA (as stated in the reports)
L1   ESO answers to E3C questions (Appendix M, data available on 28 August 2019): the majority of
     distribution connected generation provides no indication of proposed output, and no actual output
     data to the ESO.
L2   Ofgem 3.45: most DNOs only record information on generation volumes on their networks on a
     half-hourly basis, obscuring shorter-term events; the data DNOs provided gives only a partial view of
     which distributed generators tripped off or reduced output, so volumes lost at different locations
     and their causes cannot be ascertained with confidence from it.
L3   Ofgem 3.37: the information DNOs collect and record on distributed generation is variable or
     severely limited; the exact causes and timeline of the incident cannot be fully established.
L4   Ofgem, footnote 19: it has not been possible to fully validate the ESO estimate with the DNOs, as
     they also do not monitor output from distributed generators in real-time.
L5   Ofgem, footnote 31: Ofgem ascertained the distributed generation losses in section 2 of its report
     based on its validation of the frequency event modelling carried out by the ESO.

PART 3 — PUBLISHED ESTIMATES BY SOURCE (in each source's own words for timing, stage and basis; not
summed, grouped or reconciled)
ESO technical report dated 6 September 2019
E1   Table 1 (timeline): 16:52:33 [reported] approximately 150 MW [estimated] of embedded generation trips
     on vector-shift protection.
E2   Table 1 (timeline): 16:52:34 [reported] approximately 350 MW [estimated] of embedded generation trips
     on RoCoF protection [1,481MW cumulative infeed loss] [reported] (bracket as printed).
E3   Figure 2 annotation: increase in transformer loadings (Loss Of Mains) ~500 MW [estimated], labelled
     [16:52:34] [reported].
E4   Figure 2 annotation: embedded gen. loss 200 MW [modelled] @49Hz.
E5   section 4.2: post-event power system studies by ESO indicate that, for an event such as this, a loss
     of embedded generation on vector shift protection of approximately 150 MW [estimated] would be
     expected.
E6   section 4.2: based on the 150 MW [estimated] vector shift figure plus the data provided by the DNOs,
     approximately 350 MW [estimated] was lost due to RoCoF.
E7   section 4.2: a number of embedded generators and demand customers advised that their protection
     operated when the frequency reached 49 Hz [reported]; the net effect of this disconnection has been
     modelled as a 200 MW [modelled] loss of generation; protection operating at this frequency was not
     expected and has not previously been observed.
E8   footnote 2: ESO simulation data indicates that the overall total embedded generation loss could be
     slightly higher (580 MW [modelled] v 500 MW [estimated]).
E9   section 7: levels of embedded generation tripping due to RoCoF and vector shift were broadly in line
     with what was expected.
E10  section 8: during the event, approximately 500 MW [estimated] of embedded generation tripped on Loss
     of Mains protection (vector shift and Rate of Change of Frequency).
E11  Appendix I: the vector shift loss of 150 MW [estimated] is estimated to have occurred at the time of
     the circuit trip.
E12  Appendix I: based on the DNO data the RoCoF volume was 350 MW [estimated]; analysis of the simulation
     data indicates it may be slightly higher at 430 MW [modelled].
E13  Appendix I: modelling indicates that an additional 581 MW [modelled] of embedded generation was also
     disconnected, either part of the LFDD scheme or via another mechanism, resulting in a net reduction
     in demand of 350 MW [modelled].
ESO answers to E3C questions (Appendix M; data available on 28 August 2019)
E14  Answer 7: approximately 500 MW [estimated] of embedded generation was lost in the incident, estimated
     from the change in flows between the transmission and distribution networks in metered data from the
     ESO's IEMS system, corrected for the frequency characteristics of demand and for frequency response
     services in the distribution network; further analysis was to determine whether a split between RoCoF
     and vector shift could be made.
E3C interim report (October 2019)
E15  The ESO technical report states that approximately 600 MW [estimated] of embedded generation was also
     disconnected at this point, either as part of the LFDD scheme or via another mechanism, resulting in
     a net reduction in demand of 350 MW [reported].
Ofgem report dated 3 January 2020
E16  2.4.6: the frequency fell at a rate of change of frequency (RoCoF) above 0.125 Hz/s [reported]; some
     distributed generators have loss of mains protection triggered by RoCoF set at this rate; as a
     result, an estimated 350-430 MW [estimated] of distributed generation tripped off unnecessarily,
     based on information provided by the ESO.
E17  footnote 19 (to 2.4.6): this has been inferred by the ESO from a 500 MW [estimated] increase in
     transformer loadings at the interface with the distribution network; the ESO estimated
     150 MW [estimated] of vector shift and attributed the remainder to RoCoF; further ESO modelling
     suggests the total from vector shift and RoCoF could have been up to 580 MW [modelled].
E18  2.4.11 and footnote 20: there was a further net reduction in generation of 200 MW [reported] at
     49 Hz [reported]; some distributed generators tripped due to protection set to activate when the
     frequency falls to 49 Hz [reported], which could be the cause; the figure is net of demand
     disconnection, such as trains and large industrial customers.
E19  2.4.12-2.4.13: after system frequency dropped below 48.8 Hz [reported], triggering Stage 1 of LFDD,
     the ESO reported that the net demand reduction seen by the transmission system was only
     350 MW [reported]; this indicates that approximately 550 MW [estimated] of additional distributed
     generation was lost at this point.
E20  3.30: lower bound for total estimated distributed generation lost across the event is
     1,300 MW [estimated], and the loss could be as high as 1,500 MW [estimated].
E21  3.31: at least 500 MW [estimated] of distributed generation is estimated to have been lost due to
     loss of mains protection settings (RoCoF and vector shift) in the first second after the fault; some
     generators with capacities greater than 5 MW [reported] were reported to have de-loaded during the
     event and the cause is still to be determined precisely.
E22  3.32 and footnote 27: in excess of 200 MW [reported] of distributed generation tripped off when
     system frequency reached 49 Hz [reported]; significantly more may have tripped at this point, as the
     modelling is net of demand that was simultaneously disconnected such as the trains.
E3C final report (January 2020)
E23  section 1: five significant modes of embedded generator loss: vector shift, which disconnected
     approximately 150 MW [estimated]; RoCoF protection, which disconnected between 350-430 MW [reported];
     embedded generation shutting down at a frequency of 49 Hz [reported], not expected, resulting in a
     further net reduction of 200 MW [reported]; an unexpected increase in electricity demand in parallel
     with the loss of generation, attributed to the de-loading or tripping of 100 MW [reported] of
     embedded generation, the cause unknown at present; and the final loss, as reported in the ESO
     technical report, of 550 MW [reported], when the LFDD scheme was triggered. In total across the
     event, the loss of embedded generation is estimated to be in the range of
     1300 MW to 1500 MW [estimated].

Owner/originator: Distribution Network Operators (returns as tabulated by National Grid ESO and the E3C)
Record type: reconstructed per-area LFDD returns, DNO-reported relay observations and attributed annotations

PART 3 — DNO STATEMENTS AS PUBLISHED
G1   ESO technical report, Table 1 (source column: DNOs): 16:53:49.398 [reported] Frequency breaches
     48.8 Hz [reported] trigger level resulting in LFDD. 931 MW [reported] of demand is automatically
     disconnected.
G2   ESO technical report, section 4.3: the DNOs have indicated that 931 MW (3.2%) [reported] of demand
     was automatically disconnected by the operation of the LFDD scheme.
G3   E3C interim report: post event, two [reported] DNOs reported that a number of LFDD stage 1 schemes
     did not trigger, and therefore did not disconnect demand. The report gives two possible reasons:
     the system frequency did not stay at 48.8 Hz [reported] long enough to trigger the operation of all
     LFDD schemes; or the +/-0.01 Hz [reported] tolerance setting on the LFDD schemes, which meant that
     when the system frequency fell to 48.792 Hz [reported], not all schemes were triggered.
G4   E3C interim report: disconnections were also experienced in Scotland, where LFDD stage 1 schemes are
     meant to be triggered when the system frequency falls to 48.5 Hz [reported]; this was confirmed to
     be due to incorrect LFDD settings that have subsequently been corrected.
G5   E3C final report (January 2020): the DNOs have indicated that 4.0% [reported] of demand was actually
     disconnected, equating to over 1 million [reported] customers.

PART 4 — POST-EVENT ANNOTATIONS (attributed; added after the event, not return content)
Annotation A — ESO technical report dated 6 September 2019, section 4.3:
A1   The LFDD process worked largely as expected. While the process provided slightly lower than
     5% [reported] of demand, this did not materially impact the function of the LFDD in returning the
     frequency to normal operational parameters.
Annotation B — Ofgem report dated 3 January 2020:
B1   2.4.12: frequency dropping below 48.8 Hz [reported] triggered DNOs to disconnect approximately
     5% [reported] of demand (Stage 1 of LFDD); 892 MW [reported] of net demand was disconnected in
     total from the local distribution networks.
B2   2.5: in total 892 MW [reported] of net demand was disconnected as a result of LFDD, representing
     approximately 4% [reported] of national demand and affecting 1.15 million [reported] customers.
B3   3.39: on average, the DNOs disconnected an estimated 4% [estimated] of demand as measured prior to
     the event, and some disconnected significantly less than 5% [reported].
B4   3.40: the principal cause of the lower levels of demand disconnection appears to be the technical
     specification of some LFDD relays which prevented them from activating; these relays would have
     activated if the frequency had dropped marginally lower, and the Grid Code permits this margin of
     error. Another cause may have been the disconnection of significant volumes of distributed
     generation as part of the LFDD operation, which lowered the net demand reduction.
B5   3.36: some DNOs disconnected distributed generation via LFDD that was providing either frequency
     response or reserve services.
B6   3.43: Eastern Power Networks plc and South Eastern Power Networks plc (both owned by UK Power
     Networks) reconnected sites without being told to do so by the ESO, and acknowledge that they do
     not appear to have technically met the requirements of the Grid Code (Ofgem cites Grid Code
     Operation Code 6.6.4); Ofgem states these instances were caused by the configuration of the DNOs'
     operational systems.
B7   3.44: SP Distribution erroneously disconnected 22 MW [reported] in Scotland when system frequency
     fell below 48.8 Hz [reported] and reconnected customers without informing the ESO; the
     disconnection occurred due to an incorrect setting in the DNO's LFDD equipment.
Annotation C — E3C final report (January 2020):
C1   Approximately 900 MW [reported] of demand was disconnected by LFDD stage one, shared out across the
     different DNOs in England and Wales.
C2   The E3C writes that stage one should have resulted in around 5% [reported] of national demand
     being disconnected, while the DNOs indicated 4.0% [reported]. Reasons it gives: the 5% [reported]
     demand figure is based on forecasted peak demand during an average cold spell; the frequency did
     not drop below 48.8 Hz [reported] for long enough to trigger the relays to operate; and the growth
     of embedded generation connected to the distribution network.
